Temper

/TEM-per/ — rhymes with remember · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A person's temper is their tendency to lose control of their emotions in sudden flashes of anger.

He lost his temper when the referee made an unfair call.

Worked Example

A coach is known for shouting at players, slamming clipboards, and nearly getting ejected from games whenever calls go against his team.

Temper captures not just the coach's anger but his characteristic quickness to lose emotional control. We're seeing his tendency to explode — that's his nature. Temper means this is who he is, not just a one-time angry outburst. That's more precise than simply saying 'his anger.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

anger: the hot feeling of displeasure itself

irritability: being easily annoyed by small things

volatility: tendency to shift moods suddenly, explosively

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

composure: calm self-control kept under pressure

equanimity: steady, even-minded calm nothing can rattle

Where it sits · how fully annoyance boils into outbursts — impatience → irritability → testiness → temper

impatience vs. temper: Impatience is far weaker than a temper: an impatient person just hates waiting, while someone with a temper erupts into real anger.

irritability vs. temper: Irritability is weaker than a temper — it means small things annoy you easily, but a temper means those annoyances boil over into outbursts.

testiness vs. temper: Testiness is stronger than plain irritability but still weaker than a temper; a testy person snaps grumpily, while a person with a temper truly loses control.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — temper

Root — temper: to mix in due proportion; to moderate, restrain (Latin (temperare, borrowed into Old English as temprian))

Put it together

Put it together: The whole word is the Latin root temperare, 'to mix in the right proportion; to moderate or restrain.' Your temper was originally your inner 'mixture' of moods kept in balance — so when that balance tips and anger takes over, we say you lose your temper.

Use the root in a new word: temperate

Use the root in a new word: temperate: The temperate climate stayed mild and moderate all year, never swinging to extremes of heat or cold.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Temper describes a characteristic tendency to lose emotional control, while anger describes the feeling itself. When someone 'has a bad temper,' you're describing their nature; when they 'feel anger,' you're describing a momentary emotion. Use temper when talking about a person's emotional pattern or how they typically respond when provoked.
